ledger_entries.verdict: confirmed by direct re-read of the current implementation -- 009's NP-hard-modularity argument is CORRECT, not merely repeated: this is real greedy modularity optimization, not connected-components or any other decidable algorithm

rust_side.symbol: SocialNetwork::community_detection (function body cites itself: "Detect communities using Louvain algorithm (simplified greedy version)"), helper SocialNetwork::modularity_gain
rust_side.algorithm_confirmed: NOT connected components. Every node starts in its OWN singleton community (communities.insert(node.id, idx)). Then a bounded (MAX_ITERATIONS = 10) greedy local-search loop repeatedly tries moving each node to a neighboring community and accepts the move iff modularity_gain(...) > best_gain, i.e. it is hill-climbing on a modularity-style objective, exactly the Louvain local-moving phase (without the aggregation/coarsening phase Louvain normally repeats). modularity_gain computes (new_comm_edge_weight - old_comm_edge_weight) for the moving node -- a real (simplified, degree-normalization omitted) modularity delta, not a connectivity test.
rust_side.why_this_matters: Confirms this is genuinely an optimization procedure over a combinatorial partition space (set-partition of nodes into communities), which is exactly the NP-hard-in-general problem class (modularity maximization is NP-hard, Brandes et al. 2008) -- not a trivially decidable structural query like connected-components would be.

ledger_entries.verdict: confirmed by direct re-read of the current implementation -- computes a DFG via a GREEDY min-cost edge-resolution heuristic over precede-succeed and duration statistics, not a simple decidable iff-property and not an exact optimal-assignment algorithm either

rust_side.symbol: mine_correlation (lines 115-232), compute_ps_matrix (precede-succeed matrix, lines ~280-308), compute_duration_matrix (lines ~310-338), resolve_edges (greedy cost-minimisation, lines 396-440+)
rust_side.algorithm_confirmed: This performs CASE-ID-FREE correlation mining: flattens all events (ignoring case IDs), sorts by timestamp, then for each pair of distinct activities (i, j) computes a precede-succeed fraction PS[i][j] (fraction of i's end-times that precede some j start-time) and a duration statistic dur[i][j] (greedy FIFO/LIFO-matched average gap, capped by a threshold). resolve_edges then builds a cost = dur[i][j] / ps[i][j] / min(count_i, count_j) for every candidate (i,j) pair with ps[i][j] > 0, SORTS candidates by ascending cost, and greedily assigns edge frequency by consuming remaining in/out degree budget per activity (out_rem[i], in_rem[j]), skipping a direction if the reverse precede-succeed fraction is comparably strong (cycle-avoidance heuristic, ps[j][i] >= ps[i][j] * 0.8).
rust_side.why_this_matters: This is a greedy heuristic assignment over a real-valued cost function with a cycle-avoidance tie-break threshold (the 0.8 constant) -- not a closed-form decidable predicate like handover/working-together, and not provably optimal (greedy min-cost matching with degree-budget consumption is not guaranteed to find a global-min-cost assignment in general, and no optimality claim is made anywhere in the Rust code or its doc comments). There is no simple 'edge (a,b) exists iff <predicate over the trace>' law to state, because edge existence depends on the RELATIVE ranking of candidate costs across the WHOLE activity universe, not a local, position-based fact about any one pair.
